}}'''Stephen John Blundell''' (born 1967)<ref name=LibraryOfCongress/> is a professor of [[physics]] at the [[University of Oxford]]. He was previously head of [[Condensed Matter Physics]] at Oxford, and is also a professorial [[fellow]] of [[Mansfield College, Oxford]]. His research is concerned with using [[muon]]-spin rotation and [[magnetoresistance]] techniques to study a range of organic and inorganic materials, particularly those showing interesting magnetic, superconducting, or dynamical properties.<ref name=scopus/>

==Education==
Blundell completed both his undergraduate and graduate studies at the [[University of Cambridge]], attending [[Peterhouse, Cambridge]] for his undergraduate degree in [[physics]] and [[theoretical physics]] and doing his [[PhD]] at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] at Cambridge.<ref name=bphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=http://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=44CAM_ALMA21431180850003606&context=L&vid=44CAM_PROD&search_scope=SCOP_CAM_ALL&tab=cam_lib_coll&lang=en_US|title=Spin-dependent transport in artificial structures|first= Stephen John|last=Blundell|date=1993|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.309331}}|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|oclc=557401624}}</ref>

==Career and research==
He was subsequently offered a [[Science and Engineering Research Council]] (SERC) [[research fellow]]ship which involved a move to the [[Clarendon Laboratory]] at Oxford; he was later awarded a junior research fellowship at [[Merton College, Oxford]], where he began research in organic magnets and superconductors using muon-spin rotation. In 1997 he was appointed to a [[Lecturer|university lectureship]] in the Oxford Physics Department and a tutorial fellowship at [[Mansfield College, Oxford]], and was subsequently promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]].{{when|date=February 2018}} In 2004 he was awarded the title of Professor of Physics.<ref>[http://www.ox.ac.uk/gazette/2004-5/supps/1_4706.htm "Recognition of Distinction 2003-2004"], Supplement (1) to ''The Oxford University Gazette'', no. 4706 (23 September 2004). Retrieved 20 November 2016.</ref>

Blundell has authored textbooks, the first being ''Magnetism in Condensed Matter'',<ref>
{{Cite book
|title=Magnetism in Condensed Matter
|last1=Blundel|first1=Stephen
|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]
|year=2001
|isbn=9780198505914}}</ref> 
which covers the quantum mechanical nature of magnetism. He has co-authored, with his wife and colleague, astrophysicist [[Katherine Blundell]] of [[St John's College, Oxford]], a textbook entitled ''Concepts in Thermal Physics''.<ref name=citp/> It provides an introduction to the topics of thermal physics and statistical mechanics covered in a typical undergraduate course in physics. Additionally, he has authored the ''Superconductivity: A Very Short Introduction'',<ref>{{Cite book
|title=Superconductivity: A Very Short Introduction
|last1=Blundel|first1=Stephen
|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]
|year=2009
|isbn=9780199540907}}</ref>
part of the [[Very Short Introductions]] series published by [[Oxford University Press]]. He has co-authored pedagogical books on both quantum field theory and general relativity with Tom Lancaster. 

He has authored or co-authored over 300 articles<ref name=scopus>{{Scopus id}}</ref> ranging right across the world of [[solid-state physics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://users.ox.ac.uk/~sjb/publications.html|website=users.ox.ac.uk|title=Stephen Blundell Publications}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Blundell was a joint winner of the [[Daiwa Adrian Prize]] in 1999 for his work on organic magnets.<ref name=citp>{{Cite book|title=Concepts in thermal physics|last1=Blundell|first1=Stephen J.|last2=Blundell|first2=Katherine M.|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=2010|isbn=9780199562107|edition=2nd|location=Oxford|oclc=607907330|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199562091.001.0001 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1235139}}</ref> He was awarded the 2024 [[Institute of Physics Awards|Lawrence Bragg Medal and Prize]] "for contributions to physics scholarship and education through the publication of widely used and influential physics textbooks".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/2024-lawrence-bragg-medal-and-prize|title=2024 Lawrence Bragg Medal and Prize &#124; Institute of Physics}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Blundell lives in Oxford with his wife, Professor [[Katherine Blundell]]. In 2001, he was quoted in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' as saying, "Ultimately your marriage is more important than your career."<ref>{{cite journal |title=Love and the two-body problem |date=October 3, 2001 |last=Jamieson |first=Valerie |page=37 |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/love-and-two-body-problem|website=sciencemag.org}}</ref>
